lit.'<p>Ahora la barra se acerca <b>sin toca:
'

Now the rod comes close without touching. Its negative charges repel the free electrons in the metal, which move away towards the leaves: the top becomes positive and the bottom negative. The leaves open even though the electroscope is still neutral. When the rod moves away, the electrons return and the leaves close.

'
lit.'<p>Al frotar un <b>globo de goma</b> co:
'

When a rubber balloon is rubbed with wool, electrons pass from the wool to the balloon: the balloon becomes negative and the wool positive, with equal and opposite charges. Total charge is conserved. Which material gains electrons is given by the triboelectric series: the one lower in the list becomes negative.

'
lit.'<p>Con la barra cerca, se conecta el el:
'

With the rod nearby, the electroscope is connected to ground: the repelled electrons escape into it. The ground is disconnected and then the rod is moved away: the electroscope keeps a charge opposite to the rod’s (here, positive) and the leaves open. That is how a body is charged permanently by induction.

'
lit.'<p>La barra negativa toca la esfera del:
'

The negative rod touches the knob of the electroscope, which is metallic (a conductor). Some of its electrons move onto the electroscope and spread through the metal down to the leaves, which get charge of the same sign and repel: they open. When the rod is removed the electroscope stays charged with the same sign as the rod.

'
lit.'<p>La materia está formada por átomos c:
'

Matter is made of atoms with protons (+) in the nucleus and electrons (−) around it. A body is neutral when it has as many protons as electrons. It becomes charged when it gains electrons (becomes negative) or loses them (becomes positive). Only electrons move: protons do not leave the nucleus.

'
lit.'<p>Las cargas del <b>mismo signo se rep:
'

Charges of the same sign repel and charges of opposite sign attract. The force is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance: F = k·q₁·q₂/r², with k = 9·10⁹ N·m²/C². If the distance is halved, the force becomes four times larger.

'
